query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a rapid thermal annealing (RTA) process to FeCoNi-based high‐entropy thin films deposited on a rigid Si/SiO2 substrate will induce substrate‐mediated lattice strain that triggers a symmetry‐lowering chemical ordering (L10‐like phase) in the alloy, thereby enhancing magnetocrystalline anisotropy and increasing the coercivity relative to the disordered fcc baseline through the ordering effect.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi-based high entropy alloy (extended to ≥5 elements if needed to reach a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R) in a disordered face‐centered cubic (fcc) solid solution state, exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-deposited thin films on a rigid Si/SiO2 substrate to a rapid thermal annealing cycle using a brief high-temperature pulse that leverages substrate-induced strain to drive symmetry lowering and chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Thin film samples deposited on substrates that impose significant strain; RTA parameters (temperature, time, and cooling rate) are selected to favor the transformation to a low-symmetry, chemically ordered phase while preserving high configurational entropy, applicable in film geometries where substrate effects are pronounced.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a chemically ordered, low-symmetry (L10‐like) phase arising from directional lattice distortion induced by the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The substrate-induced strain during RTA breaks the cubic symmetry of the fcc FeCoNi matrix, promoting atomic rearrangements into an L10-like structure. This ordering effect enhances spin–orbit coupling and magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby reinforcing domain wall pinning and resulting in a higher coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited disordered fcc FeCoNi-based alloy (with low coercivity on the order of ~10 Oe), the RTA-treated film is expected to exhibit a significantly increased coercivity (potentially one to two orders of magnitude higher) while retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeCoNi-based thin films in a single fcc phase with high Ms and low coercivity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply to thin film specimens where substrate-induced strain is effective; bulk casts without a constraining substrate might not achieve the same ordering or coercivity enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the coercivity increase and the degree of chemical ordering depend on the exact RTA conditions and film thickness. Further tuning of composition (to include additional elements that maintain high configurational entropy) may be needed to optimize the balance between ordering and magnetic properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy thin films on Si/SiO2 substrates. One set is processed by a rapid thermal annealing protocol designed to induce substrate strain, and the other set is left as-deposited. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to identify any symmetry lowering or ordering, and measure magnetic properties using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) to record hysteresis loops.
measurements: XRD for superlattice peaks or splitting indicative of L10-like ordering
TEM for microstructural evidence of ordered domains and lattice distortions
Magnetic hysteresis loops to quantify coercivity, saturation magnetization, and anisotropy fields
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA‐treated thin films do not exhibit clear structural signs of chemical ordering (i.e., no L10-like features or significant lattice distortion) and if the measured coercivity is not significantly higher (neither 10× nor more) than that of the as-deposited films, then the hypothesis that substrate-induced strain during RTA induces an ordered phase resulting in enhanced coercivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling.
